details:
**"Cross of Gold" speech**
Bryan's 1896 speech at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago attacking the gold standard and championing free silver. It won him the presidential nomination and is the most famous giveaway for him.

**"You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold"**
The closing line of the Cross of Gold speech, preceded by "You shall not press down upon the brow of labor this crown of thorns." Earlier in the speech he declared "we have petitioned, and our petitions have been scorned" and warned that if farms were destroyed "the grass will grow in the streets of every city in the country."

**Free silver and 16 to 1**
Bryan's central cause was bimetallism, the unlimited coinage of silver at a ratio of 16 ounces of silver to 1 ounce of gold. The inflationary policy appealed to indebted farmers in the West and South; cartoons showed him carrying a bag labeled "16 to 1."

**Scopes Trial and Clarence Darrow**
In 1925 Bryan helped prosecute John Scopes for teaching evolution in violation of Tennessee's Butler Act. Defense attorney Clarence Darrow famously called Bryan to the stand as a Bible expert, questioning him about Adam and Eve and the date of the Great Flood. Bryan won the case but died five days later.

**Resignation over the Lusitania**
Bryan was Woodrow Wilson's first Secretary of State, but he resigned in 1915 because he felt Wilson's strong protest notes to Germany after the sinking of the RMS Lusitania endangered U.S. neutrality. He was replaced by Robert Lansing.

**1896 election and William McKinley**
Bryan lost the 1896 election (and again in 1900) to Republican William McKinley, whose manager Mark Hanna ran a well-funded "front porch campaign" from McKinley's home in Canton, Ohio. At 36, Bryan was the youngest major-party presidential nominee ever.

**Three-time Democratic nominee**
Bryan was the Democratic presidential nominee in 1896, 1900, and 1908, losing each time; his 1908 loss was to William Howard Taft. His running mates included Arthur Sewall (1896) and John Kern (1908).

**Populist fusion and Thomas Watson**
In 1896 the Populist Party also nominated Bryan, but chose Georgia's Thomas Watson as his running mate instead of the Democrats' Arthur Sewall. Gold-standard Bourbon Democrats bolted to form the National Democratic Party, nominating John Palmer.

**The Commoner and "The Great Commoner"**
After his 1896 loss Bryan founded and published a newspaper called The Commoner, which pushed reforms such as railroad regulation. "The Great Commoner" and "The Boy Orator of the Platte" were his nicknames.

**"The Prince of Peace" and the Chautauqua circuit**
Bryan was a hugely popular lecturer on the Chautauqua circuit, where his speeches included "The Prince of Peace," which grounded morality in religion and criticized evolution, and "The Value of an Ideal."

**"Cooling-off" treaties**
As Secretary of State, Bryan negotiated arbitration treaties with about 30 nations requiring disputes to be referred to an international commission before any war. He gave signatories paperweights shaped like plowshares made from melted-down swords.

**Bryan–Chamorro Treaty**
A 1914 treaty with Nicaragua, negotiated with Emiliano Chamorro, that gave the United States exclusive rights to build a canal through Nicaragua and to lease bases there.

**"Shall the People Rule?"**
Bryan's slogan in the 1908 campaign against Taft, during which he also advocated citizenship for Puerto Ricans. Opponents quipped that "you can vote for Bryan anytime" given how often he ran.

**Anti-imperialism and the Philippines**
Although he supported the Spanish-American War, Bryan opposed annexing the Philippines and made imperialism a theme of his 1900 campaign, including a speech warning against the "flag of an empire."

**1896 convention: Altgeld and Richard Bland**
At the 1896 Chicago convention, Illinois governor John Peter Altgeld helped swing delegates to Bryan, who overtook front-runner Richard "Silver Dick" Bland on the fifth ballot to win the nomination.
